title: Al-Ghazali's crisis
hook: the famous scholar leaves his post in doubt and finds the living path (Deliverance from Error)

segments.voice: Yesterday, Junayd of Baghdad, the master of sobriety, who tied the inner path to the Qur'an and the sunnah. Your line was sober love. Did you come back and do the next ordinary thing well? Day two hundred ninety-seven.

A professor at the top of his field. Students crowding his lectures, rulers asking his opinion, his books read everywhere. And one day he stands up to teach, and can't speak. His tongue won't move. He can't eat. The doctors examine him and say it isn't his body; it's something in his heart. That happened in Baghdad, in the year 1095, to a celebrated scholar. He wrote about it himself, later, in a short book about his search for certainty. Today, his crisis.
screen: `AT THE TOP OF HIS FIELD.` → `HE STANDS TO TEACH, AND CAN'T.` → `BAGHDAD, 1095.`

segments.voice: His name was Abu Hamid al-Ghazali. He was a master of law, theology and philosophy, and he taught at the Nizamiyya, the great college of Baghdad. In his book, called Deliverance from Error, he says he'd started doubting how anyone can know anything for certain, and he went through every school he could find: the theologians, the philosophers, the ones who claimed secret teachers. Finally he turned to the Sufis, read their books, and understood them. And he realized something. He could explain their path perfectly, and he hadn't walked a single step of it. He gives an example. There's a difference, he says, between knowing the definition of health and being healthy, between knowing what makes a person full and actually being full. The Sufi word for the second kind of knowing is dhawq, tasting. As if he could describe honey without ever having tasted it. And he saw that his fame, his salary and his reputation were the very things holding him back. That's when his tongue stopped. So he gave away his wealth, except what his family needed, and left Baghdad quietly. He spent years traveling, to Damascus, Jerusalem and the holy cities, praying, keeping silent, practicing. In those years he wrote his great work, the Revival of the Religious Sciences, joining the law and the inner path in one book. Later Muslims called him Hujjat al-Islam, the proof of Islam. It started with admitting a doubt. Knowing is not tasting.
screen: `DELIVERANCE FROM ERROR.` · `HE COULD EXPLAIN IT, NOT WALK IT.` · `DHAWQ — TASTING.` · `HE GAVE IT UP AND LEFT.` · then, large: `KNOWING IS NOT TASTING.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: admit one doubt honestly. Sit, and breathe. Think of something you're supposed to be sure of, about faith, your work, a relationship, yourself, and let yourself notice where you're actually unsure. Don't solve it. Don't panic. Al-Ghazali's doubt was the door, not the end. Just name it plainly to yourself. If you pray, you can bring the doubt to God as it is. If you don't, just let it sit beside you without arguing. The bell holds the time.
Al-Ghazali's crisis. The great scholar who lost his voice, left his post, and went looking to taste what he knew. Today's word.
Your line: knowing is not tasting. Today, pick one thing you know a lot about and actually do it, instead of explaining it. Day two hundred ninety-seven.

howItsDone: Al-Ghazali's Revival of the Religious Sciences is still read in mosques and study circles, and his account of his crisis is often taught as a model of honest searching within the faith.

fork.setup: you're a celebrated scholar in Baghdad. you can explain the Sufi path perfectly, but you've never walked it, and now you can't speak. what do you do?
options: rest a while, then return to lecturing.
give away your wealth and leave to practice what you know.
write a book refuting the Sufis.
fork.reveal: he gave away his wealth, left Baghdad quietly, and spent years in prayer and practice, then wrote the Revival.

original.note: Arabic: taste, tasting; in Sufi writing, knowing by direct experience.

trapdoor: what you thought: a scholar lost his faith.
what it means: a scholar found he knew about the path without having tasted it, and left everything to walk it.
what a scholar hears: al-Munqidh min al-Dalal; the Nizamiyya of Baghdad, 1095; the health and satiety analogy for dhawq.

notes: Details of the crisis (tongue unable to speak, loss of appetite, physicians' verdict, 1095 at the Nizamiyya) and the analogy of health/satiety are from memory of al-Munqidh; confirm. His own analogy also uses drunkenness.
Travel route (Damascus, Jerusalem, Hebron, Mecca and Medina) and 'years' (about a decade before returning to teach at Nishapur) simplified; confirm.
The Claud Field 1909 English translation is public domain but not on the validator's list, so nothing is quoted.

Editor review (2026-10-01): SERIOUS fix: the Revival (Ihya') was written during his years away, not after he came back. Hook no longer opens 'Imagine' or uses second person for his story; cut 'the most famous scholar in the Muslim world', 'the most important college', 'hundreds of students' and 'across the Muslim world'. The 1095 date is in al-Munqidh (Rajab 488 AH).
